query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A targeted in‐situ, short-duration, low‐temperature heat treatment applied immediately after each powder deposition layer during AM of AlCrFeNiSi will significantly relieve residual thermal stresses, promote a more uniform metastable microstructure, and thereby improve the mechanical properties relative to components produced solely under conventional high-thermal-load conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: As-processed AlCrFeNiSi components manufactured via standard high-thermal-load additive manufacturing, which exhibit high residual thermal stresses, non-uniform grain structures, and degraded mechanical properties.
generation.intervention: Integrate an in-situ low-temperature heat treatment step (e.g., by controlled laser preheating or interlayer dwell heating) immediately following each layer deposition during the AM process.
generation.conditions: Processing a miniature component (characteristic dimensions <10 mm) using a laser powder bed fusion system with build plate pre-heated to approximately 600°C and an interlayer dwell time adjusted to achieve an effective post-deposition heat treatment of around 10 minutes per layer. Tests are to be conducted in a controlled inert atmosphere and compared with samples produced under conventional high-thermal-load settings.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced residual stresses and a refined, metastable microstructure with more evenly distributed grain sizes and fewer epitaxial columnar grains.
generation.mechanism: The controlled, lower-temperature heat treatment minimizes steep thermal gradients during solidification. This permits stress relaxation and controlled phase evolution, leveraging metastable phase formation to avoid excessive grain coarsening while ensuring mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated specimens will exhibit lower measured residual stresses (as detected by XRD), improved mechanical properties (e.g., increased yield strength and ductility), and a more homogeneous microstructure compared to specimens made under conventional high-thermal-load conditions.
generation.baseline: Components produced using standard high-thermal-load AM conditions without any intermediate heat treatment, known to develop significant residual stresses, nonuniform microstructures, and compromised mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The intervention is hypothesized to be effective for miniature components where rapid heat dissipation is manageable; its efficacy may diminish for larger builds or geometries that exacerbate thermal gradients, and the optimum temperature/time window may be specific to the AlCrFeNiSi composition.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of stress reduction, the optimal heat treatment temperature and duration, and the extent of mechanical property improvement remain uncertain and need to be empirically determined for the specific alloy system.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of AlCrFeNiSi miniature components under identical AM conditions: one set with the in-situ low-temperature heat treatment intervention and one without (conventional process). Subsequent sample analysis should be performed on both sets.
measurements: Residual stress measurement via X-ray diffraction (XRD)
Microstructural analysis using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to quantify grain size and phase uniformity
Mechanical testing via nanoindentation and tensile tests to evaluate yield strength and ductility
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the in-situ heat-treated components do not show a statistically significant reduction in residual stress (e.g., less than 10% compared to the baseline) and corresponding improvements in grain uniformity and mechanical properties (yield strength and ductility) relative to conventionally processed specimens, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

Harnessing metastability for grain size control in multiprincipal element alloys during additive manufacturing

Abstract: Controlling microstructure in fusion-based metal additive manufacturing (AM) remains a significant challenge due to the many parameters that directly impact solidification condition. Multiprincipal element alloys (MPEAs), also known as high entropy alloys, offer a vast compositional space to design for microstructural engineering due to their chemical complexity and exceptional properties. Here, we use the FeMnCoCr system as a model platform for exploring alloy design in MPEAs for AM. By exploiting the decreasing stability of the face-centered cubic phase with increasing Mn content, we achieve notable grain refinement and breakdown of epitaxial columnar grain growth. We employ a multifaceted approach encompassing thermodynamic modeling, operando synchrotron X-ray diffraction, multiscale microstructural characterization, and mechanical testing to gain insight into the solidification physics and its ramifications on the resulting microstructure of FeMnCoCr MPEAs. Effect of Heat Treatment Duration on the Recrystallization and Electrochemical Properties of Cold-Rolled Cantor-Type High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs), such as the Cantor alloy, are considered for various structural applications owing to their excellent corrosion resistance and high strength at low temperatures, typically below −70 °C, including cryogenic conditions. However, during metalworking, introducing stresses and grain refinement can reduce the corrosion resistance of HEAs. Recrystallization heat treatment relieves these stresses and homogenizes the grain structure, thereby restoring their corrosion resistance and physical properties. However, inadequate heat treatment can result in a microstructure in which coarse and refined grains coexist; thus, the corrosion resistance is diminished and the physical properties are compromised. Therefore, a proper heat treatment is essential for achieving the desired corrosion resistance and mechanical properties of HEAs. Design and Fabrication of New High Entropy Alloys for Evaluating Titanium Replacements in Additive Manufacturing

Abstract: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) were prepared using the powder bed fusion (PBF) technique. Among titanium free alloys AlCoCrFeNiMn, CoCr1.3FeMnNi0.7, AlCoCrFeNi1.3, and AlCoCr1.3FeNi1.3 have been further investigated. A cost comparison was done for these four alloys as well as the titanium-based alloys AlCoCrFeNiTi and AlCo0.8CrFeNiTi. Such a comparison was done in order to evaluate the performance of the titanium-free alloys as the estimated cost of these will be less than for Ti-based HEAs. Hence, we have chosen four titanium free alloys and two titanium-based alloys for further processing. All these alloys were fabricated and subsequently characterized for phase, purity and performance. Scanning electron microscopy-based images were captured for microstructure characterization. EIS-based tests and potentiodynamic scans were performed to evaluate corrosion current. Hardness tests were performed for mechanical properties evaluation.
